entries.modern_form: Taino (Arawakan, Greater Antilles) tabago / tabaco 'tube for inhaling smoke; roll of tobacco leaves'
entries.note: Klein p.1623 s.v. tobacco is verbatim Nourai's root: 'Taino (Caribbean) tabaco, “pipe for smoking; roll of tobacco leaves”'. The language label the book prints, 'Caribian', is Nourai's spelling for Caribbean/Arawakan; the donor language is properly Taino (Arawakan), the language of Hispaniola, not Cariban proper. Modern dictionaries split on the exact sense: Oviedo (1535) reported it as the pipe, Las Casas (1552) as the roll of leaves, and Etymonline/Wiktionary prefer Las Casas; the current AHD adds that Spanish tabaco is 'partly from Old Spanish atabaca, altabaca' < Arabic al-ṭubbāq (Inula viscosa), which is exactly the claim Nourai's own NOTE on node #4 attributes to AHD:1350 — so that note is a faithful report of AHD and is still AHD's view.
entries.note_fa: ریشهٔ این خانواده واژهٔ تاینویی (از زبان‌های آراواکی جزایر کارائیب) tabaco/tabago است به معنای «نای دودکش یا لولهٔ برگ توتون پیچیده». کلاین (ص‌۱۶۲۳) دقیقاً همین را می‌آورد؛ برچسب «Caribian» که نورایی به کار برده املای شخصی اوست و زبان وام‌دهنده درست‌تر «تاینو» است. فرهنگ AHD امروز هم می‌گوید بخشی از tabaco اسپانیایی به اسپانیایی کهن atabaca و از آن‌جا به عربی الطُبّاق بازمی‌گردد؛ پس یادداشت نورایی دربارهٔ AHD نقل درستی است. ادعای نورایی دربارهٔ ریشه درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 861 (0-based 860), s.v. tobacco: 'Sp., Port. tabaco, fr. Taino (Caribbean) tabaco, “pipe for smoking; roll of tobacco leaves”; the English form of the word was prob. influenced by Tobago, name of a West Indian island; cp. F. tabac, It. tobacco, G. Tabak, Du. tabak, Hind. tambaka, which all derive ult. fr. Taino tabaco. Cp. also tabatiere.' — every box of Nourai's chart except the Persian one comes from this single entry.

consulted.note: 'Tobacco. (Span.-Hayti.) Span. tabaco. A word taken from the language of Hayti (Clavigero, Hist. of Mexico).'
'[The word tabaco is from the language of Hayti, and meant, first, the pipe, secondly, the plant, thirdly, the sleep which followed its use (Mr. J. Platt, 9 ser. N. & Q. viii. 322).]'

'Spanish tabaco, probably partly from a Taíno word recorded by a Spanish chronicler as tabago, a tube for inhaling smoke… and partly from Old Spanish atabaca, altabaca… from Arabic al-ṭubbāq' — a double etymology, so the Caribbean root is only half the story for AHD.

consulted.where: LKT.txt (Lokotsch) — no numbered entry for tabak/tabaco
consulted.note: grep 'tabak|tabaco' finds only compounds (Rauchtabak, tabak 'Gerber' no. 1195, tk. tabak 'Sohle' no. 1962a); Lokotsch has no entry for tobacco because he covers only oriental loans.

nodes.derivation: NP تنباکو tanbākū 'tobacco' is a 17th-century colonial Wanderwort, but not a direct Persian borrowing from Taino as the arrow from the root box implies. Tobacco reached Safavid Iran c. 1600 by way of the Portuguese Estado da Índia (Hormuz/Goa) and Mughal India — Shah ʿAbbās I banned smoking in 1030/1621 — and the Persian form goes back to Portuguese tabaco through the Indian shape tambākū/tambākū: Wiktionary derives تنباکو straight from Portuguese tabaco. The Persian variant تمباکو that Nourai prints beside it is the Indian nasalised form, and the alternation ن/م before b is the regular Persian/Urdu writing of the labial nasal (Iranian pronunciation [tʰæm.bɑː.kʰuː]). So the etymon is right, the route is compressed: Taino → Spanish/Portuguese → India → Persia.
nodes.derivation_fa: «تنباکو» وام‌واژه‌ای است از پرتغالی tabaco که خود از زبان تاینویی جزایر کارائیب گرفته شده است؛ اما راه ورود آن به فارسی مستقیم نبوده است: توتون در حدود ۱۰۰۹/۱۶۰۰ از راه پرتغالیان هرمز و هندوستان به ایران رسید و شاه عباس اول در ۱۰۳۰ ق کشیدن آن را قدغن کرد. صورت «تمباکو» همان شکل هندی واژه است و ابدال ن/م پیش از ب در فارسی و اردو قاعده‌مند است. ادعای نورایی در اصل درست است ولی مسیر وام‌گیری را فشرده کرده است.

ref_check.note: Mo'in's entry exists and matches the gloss — via abadis.ir (فرهنگ معین): 'تنباکو (تَ) (اِ.) گیاهی است یک ساله، بومی قارهٔ امریکا که به وسیلهٔ اسپانیایی‌ها به اروپا برده شده' — but Mo'in gives no donor-language tag there, and the page number of the 6-vol Amir Kabir edition cannot be checked (only the 2-vol Adena abridgement is scanned).

consulted.note: 'گیاهی است یک ساله، بومی قارهٔ امریکا که به وسیلهٔ اسپانیایی‌ها به اروپا برده شده' — American origin confirmed.
the word appears only inside other entries ('بالای سر قلیان نهند تا تنباکو و آتش را…'; 'دخانیه… اقسام توتون و تنباکو'); the headword itself was lost in this OCR.

Dehkhoda states tobacco came to India from Europe in Akbar Shah's time and that the Spanish brought it to Europe from the island of Tabago — i.e. the Persian word arrived with the plant, from the West, not from a Caribbean language directly.
Klein lists Hind. tambaka but no Persian form; the Persian box is the one box in this chart that Klein does not cover.

nodes.derivation: Hindustani (Urdu/Hindi) تمباکو / तम्बाकू tambākū 'tobacco' is Klein's own example: he lists 'Hind. tambaka' among the forms that 'all derive ult. fr. Taino tabaco', so Nourai's arrow reproduces Klein exactly. The immediate donor, however, was Portuguese tabaco, brought to Goa and the Deccan in the late 16th century (tobacco is first recorded in India under Akbar, c. 1604–05); the intrusive -m- before b is an Indic nasalisation of the Portuguese open syllable. Wiktionary goes one step further and makes Urdu تمباکو a borrowing from Classical Persian تنباکو, which would reverse Nourai's implicit Persian/Indian parallelism; either way the ultimate source box is right.
nodes.derivation_fa: صورت هندی‌واردوی «تمباکو» همان واژهٔ تاینویی است که از راه پرتغالیان گوا در اواخر سدهٔ دهم/شانزدهم به هند رسیده است؛ کلاین نیز همین را می‌آورد. «م» میانی زادهٔ خیشومی‌شدن هجای باز در زبان‌های هندی است. ویکی‌واژه اردوی تمباکو را وام‌گرفته از فارسی تنباکو می‌داند، که اگر درست باشد جهت پیکان نورایی تغییر می‌کند. در مجموع ادعا با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 861 s.v. tobacco: '…cp. F. tabac, It. tobacco, G. Tabak, Du. tabak, Hind. tambaka, which all derive ult. fr. Taino tabaco.' The transliteration 'tambaka' in the chart is Klein's own.

consulted.note: Hobson-Jobson declines an 'elaborate article' and gives only quotations on 'the introduction of tobacco into India and the East'; it confirms the plant and word came to India from the Spanish/Portuguese world, not the reverse.
Whitworth's Anglo-Indian Dictionary has no 'tambaku'/'tobacco' entry; the word occurs only inside Bhaduri, Chilam, Hookah (lines 1030, 1626, 2867).
'Borrowed from Classical Persian تَنْبَاکُو (tanbākū)' — makes the Indian form secondary to the Persian one.

nodes.derivation: Port. tabaco 'tobacco' is one of the two Iberian forms Klein cites side by side ('Sp., Port. tabaco'); it was taken over from the Antillean Taino word in the first half of the 16th century by the same Iberian colonists who reported it (Oviedo 1535, Las Casas 1552) and carried it to Africa, India and Iran. The word is unchanged in shape: Taino tabaco → Port. tabaco, a straight substitution loan with no sound change at all.
nodes.derivation_fa: پرتغالی tabaco عیناً همان واژهٔ تاینویی است که در نیمهٔ نخست سدهٔ شانزدهم میلادی به زبان‌های شبه‌جزیرهٔ ایبری راه یافت و هیچ دگرگونی آوایی نیافت. کلاین شکل اسپانیایی و پرتغالی را هم‌عرض می‌آورد. ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 861: 'tobacco, n. — Sp., Port. tabaco, fr. Taino (Caribbean) tabaco…' — Portuguese is named explicitly.

consulted.note: Skeat names only 'Span. tabaco'; the Portuguese form is not mentioned, but nothing contradicts it.
AHD routes English through 'Spanish tabaco' only; Portuguese is not part of its chain.

nodes.derivation: Spanish tabaco itself is not in doubt — it is the form in which the Taino word entered European languages — but the arrow Portuguese → Spanish reverses the accepted priority: the earliest records are Spanish (Oviedo, Historia general 1535; Las Casas 1552), the borrowing took place in the Spanish Antilles, and Klein, Etymonline, AHD and Wiktionary all make Spanish the source (Klein prints 'Sp., Port. tabaco' side by side, not Port. > Sp.). Nourai's own NOTE on this box — that AHD:1350 derives the Spanish word from Arabic ṭabāq, 'a euphoria-causing herb' — is a fair report and still AHD's position: the current edition says tabaco is 'partly from Old Spanish atabaca, altabaca, a Mediterranean plant (Inula viscosa)… from Arabic al-ṭubbāq… from Syriac dubāqā, birdlime'. So Spanish is a blend: a Taino smoking-tube word reinforced by an existing Andalusi-Arabic herb name.
nodes.derivation_fa: خود اسپانیایی tabaco مسلّم است، امّا پیکان «پرتغالی ← اسپانیایی» تقدّم تاریخی را وارونه کرده است: کهن‌ترین شواهد (اووییدو ۱۵۳۵ و لاس‌کازاس ۱۵۵۲) اسپانیایی است و کلاین، اتیمانلاین و AHD همه اسپانیایی را سرچشمه می‌دانند. یادداشت خود نورایی دربارهٔ ریشهٔ عربی الطُبّاق نقل درستی از AHD است و همچنان در ویرایش تازه می‌ماند: واژهٔ اسپانیایی آمیزه‌ای است از واژهٔ تاینویی و نام گیاهی عربی‌اندلسی.

ref_check.note: Klein writes 'Sp., Port. tabaco' — the two are coordinated, not chained; he gives no Portuguese → Spanish direction. Klein therefore supports the word but not this arrow.

consulted.note: confirms Nourai's NOTE: '…partly from Old Spanish atabaca, altabaca… (from Arabic al-ṭubbāq: al-, the + ṭubbāq, ṭabbāq, the plant I. viscosa, from Syriac dubāqā, birdlime…)'.
'from Spanish tabaco, in part from an Arawakan language of the Caribbean' — Spanish, not Portuguese, is the transmitting language; 'The entry contains no mention of Arabic tabbaq.'
'Tobacco. (Span.-Hayti.) Span. tabaco' — Skeat's language tag puts Spanish alone between English and Hayti.

nodes.derivation: English tobacco, first attested 1580s (Klein/Etymonline; Camden 1586 on Ralph Lane bringing 'Indicam illam plantam quam Tabaccam vocant' to England), is the Spanish word taken over whole. The shift of the first vowel from ta- to to- is 18th-century and, on Klein's and Etymonline's account, was helped by the island name Tobago — which Columbus is said to have named in 1498 from a Haitian word for the pipe. Nourai's arrow Spanish → English is exactly Klein's.
nodes.derivation_fa: انگلیسی tobacco (نخستین شواهد ۱۵۸۰م) همان واژهٔ اسپانیایی است که بی‌دگرگونی وام گرفته شده؛ تبدیل ta- به to- در سدهٔ هجدهم رخ داده و به باور کلاین و اتیمانلاین زیر تأثیر نام جزیرهٔ Tobago بوده است (ریشه‌شناسی عامیانه). ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 861: 'the English form of the word was prob. influenced by Tobago, name of a West Indian island'.

the 1975 AHD page is not open online, but the current AHD entry for tobacco is the same text Nourai paraphrases ('Spanish tabaco… partly from Arabic al-ṭubbāq'), so the citation is sound in substance.

consulted.note: 'Tobacco. (Span.-Hayti.)'

consulted.where: HJB.txt s.v. TOBACCO, quotation from Camden's Annales (1586)
consulted.note: '…reduces Indicam illam plantam quam Tabaccam vocant et Nicotiam… in Angliam primi… intulerunt' — dates the English adoption.

nodes.derivation: F. tabac 'tobacco' is the Spanish word taken into French about 1600 (earlier herbe à Nicot, from Jean Nicot, who sent seeds from Lisbon to Catherine de' Medici in 1560); Klein cites 'F. tabac' among the direct reflexes of Taino tabaco. The snuffbox word in the chart, tabaquière, is not a blunder: Klein s.v. tabatiere states that modern F. tabatière comes 'fr. earlier tabaquière, fr. tabac' — a regular -ière agent/container suffix on tabac, with later dissimilation of the velar (tabaquière > tabatière).
nodes.derivation_fa: فرانسوی tabac حدود سال ۱۶۰۰ از اسپانیایی وام گرفته شد. صورت tabaquière که نورایی می‌آورد خطا نیست؛ کلاین می‌گوید tabatière امروزی از صورت کهن‌تر tabaquière (با پسوند -ière بر tabac) آمده و پس از آن کاف میانی به ت بدل شده است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 861 s.v. tobacco: '…cp. F. tabac… Cp. also tabatiere.'; and leaf 829 s.v. tabatiere: 'F., fr. earlier tabaquière, fr. tabac, “tobacco”'.

consulted.note: 'Cultivation began in France around 1556 with imported seeds' — fixes the date of the French adoption.
Pihan's dictionary of French words from Arabic/Persian/Turkish has no article on tabac (only 'tabac' in passing at line 3530, s.v. Hachighe); he did not consider it an oriental loan.

nodes.derivation: English tabatiere (also spelt tabatière) 'snuffbox' is a straight 19th-century borrowing of French tabatière, itself from earlier tabaquière 'tobacco-container', from tabac. Klein carries it as an English headword — which is why Nourai's box is English — and gives exactly this chain; the sense 'snuffbox' follows the 18th-century vogue for snuff (tabac à priser). Nourai's page reference KLN:1563 lands in the right place: Klein's tabatiere entry stands on the leaf whose running head numbers are 1564/1565 (leaf 829 of KLN_1966.txt).
nodes.derivation_fa: انگلیسی tabatiere «جعبهٔ انفیه» وام‌واژه‌ای است از فرانسوی tabatière که خود از tabaquière و در نهایت از tabac ساخته شده است؛ تحول معنایی «ظرف توتون» ← «قوطی انفیه» به رواج انفیه در سدهٔ هجدهم بازمی‌گردد. ارجاع KLN:1563 نیز درست است. ادعای نورایی درست است.

ref_check.note: KLN_1966.txt leaf 829 (running heads 1564/1565), s.v. tabatiere: 'tabatiere, n., a snuffbox. — F., fr. earlier tabaquière, fr. tabac, “tobacco”. See tobacco.' The page number is right within a page.

consulted.note: the tobacco entry itself ends 'Cp. also tabatiere', closing the loop between the two boxes.

consulted.where: FSD_vol4.txt — not separately checked for this minor headword
consulted.note: Funk & Wagnalls was not consulted for tabatiere; Klein's entry is unambiguous and no source disputes it.

entries.modern_form: New Persian تبیر / تبیره tabīr, tabīra 'drum' (dimin. تبوراک tabūrāk); Middle Persian drum word attested is tumbag
entries.note: The Iranian drum word is real and old: NP تبیر/تبیره is in Rūdakī and Ferdowsī, Mo'in glosses تبیره 'دهل، کوس، طبل، نقاره' and has a separate entry تبوراک 'طبلی کوچک', and the current AHD reconstructs 'Persian tabīr, tabīra, drum; probably akin to Middle Persian tumbag, and of imitative origin.' What is NOT attested is the headword as Nourai sets it up: MacKenzie's Concise Pahlavi Dictionary knows only tumbag 'drum' (and its index 'drum tumbag'), Nyberg only tumbak; no Pahlavi *tabūrāk is recorded anywhere. Devic, whom Nourai cites for the branch, actually calls تبوراک a late diminutive of tabūr with an intrusive alef ('lequel est, suivant toute vraisemblance, un diminutif de tabour, dans lequel s'est glissé fautivement un ا â'). So the root box should read New Persian tabīr/tabīra, not Pahlavi tabūrāk; the -āk is the New Persian diminutive suffix. A second, larger problem runs through the whole chart: Nourai fuses two different Iranian words — the drum word tabīr/ṭabl and the long-necked lute word tanbūr (MP tambūr) — into one tree.
entries.note_fa: واژهٔ ایرانی «تبیر/تبیره» به معنای دهل کهن و اصیل است و در شعر رودکی و فردوسی دیده می‌شود؛ معین نیز تبیره را «دهل، کوس، طبل، نقاره» و تبوراک را «طبلی کوچک» معنی کرده است. امّا صورت «تبوراک» در فارسی میانه (پهلوی) هیچ شاهدی ندارد: مکنزی و نیبرگ تنها tumbag/tumbak «دهل» را ضبط کرده‌اند، و پسوند -اک در تبوراک پسوند تصغیر فارسی نو است (دویک نیز آن را مصغّر tabūr می‌داند که الفی نابجا در آن راه یافته). افزون بر این، نورایی دو واژهٔ جدا را — «تبیر/طبل» (کوبه‌ای) و «تنبور» (زهی) — در یک درخت درهم آمیخته است. بنابراین ریشه با احتیاط پذیرفتنی است.

ref_check.note: Mo'in does have both words — MON_part1.txt line 37743 'تبوراک… طبلی کوچک که زارعان به جهت رمانیدن جانوران از کشتزار نوازند' and line 37757 'تبیره [= تبیر] دهل، کوس، طبل، نقاره' (the Latin-script form beside تبیره is illegible in this OCR) — but both are New Persian entries; Mo'in nowhere labels tabūrāk Pahlavi, and the page number of the 6-vol edition cannot be checked because only the 2-vol Adena abridgement is scanned.

consulted.where: PHD.txt line 597 and English index line 1701
consulted.note: MacKenzie's only Pahlavi drum is 'tumbag [twmbk' | N ~a] drum'; the index reads 'drum tumbag.' There is no tabūrāk, tabīr or ṭabl in the Concise Pahlavi Dictionary.
'tumbak [twmbk'] drum, or kettle-drum 209. — Arm. lw. tmbuk < *tumbuk “drum”; NP tanbak, tanbuk, tanbik (BQ also tun-) “bagpipe”, “drum”.' Nyberg's Pahlavi drum word is tumbak, not tabūrāk.

consulted.where: BQT_v1_pages.txt leaf 696 (ت section), s.vv. تبیره / تبیر
consulted.note: 'تبیره بر وزن نفس، دهل و کوس و نقاره و طبل را گویند'; 'تبیر… بمعنی تبیره است که دهل و کوس و طبل و نقاره باشد' — Borhān-e Qāṭeʿ confirms the New Persian word and its synonyms.
'تبیر طبل باشد، تبیره نیز گویند' — the word is already lexicalised in the oldest Persian dictionary (11th c.).

'…or perhaps ultimately from alteration… of Persian tabīr, tabīra, drum; probably akin to Middle Persian tumbag, and of imitative origin.' The Persian drum word is recognised, but the Middle Persian congener is tumbag, not *tabūrāk.

nodes.derivation: All three New Persian forms are well attested. تبیر tabīr / تبیره tabīra is the classical word for a large two-headed drum (Rūdakī's verse quoted in the box, 'پس تبیری دید نزدیک درخت…'; also Ferdowsī, Niẓāmī, Asadī Ṭūsī), and تبوراک tabūrāk is its diminutive in -āk, glossed by Mo'in as a small drum farmers beat to scare animals off the fields. The -āk suffix is the ordinary New Persian diminutive (cf. مغاک, سوراخ‌); Devic says as much, adding that the intrusive alef of tabūrāk is a scribal accretion on tabūr. The word is onomatopoeic in origin, akin to MP tumbag (MacKenzie), so 'from the root box' is trivially true — the node is the root, restated in New Persian.
nodes.derivation_fa: هر سه صورت در فارسی نو شاهد دارند: «تبیر/تبیره» دهل بزرگ دوسر است (بیت رودکی در همین جعبه، و شواهد فردوسی و اسدی طوسی) و «تبوراک» مصغّر آن با پسوند تصغیر «ـاک» است که معین آن را طبل کوچک کشاورزان برای رماندن جانوران معنی کرده است. این واژه آواواژه (مقلّد صدا) است و با tumbag پهلوی هم‌ریشه است. ادعای نورایی در این گره درست است.

ref_check.note: MON_part1.txt line 37743 'تبوراک… طبلی کوچک که زارعان به جهت رمانیدن جانوران از کشتزار نوازند. دف، دایره'; line 37757 'تبیره [= تبیر] دهل، کوس، طبل، نقاره'. Both of Nourai's Persian glosses are Mo'in's own; only the page number is uncheckable.

consulted.note: 'تبیره… دهل و کوس و نقاره و طبل را گویند'; the same leaf also has 'تبیره دهلی است که میان آن باریک و هر دو سرش پهن می‌باشد' — the two-headed drum of Mo'in's gloss.
Shahnameh lines cited under تبیره: 'همی از تبیره شود گوش کر' — the drum sense in Ferdowsī.

consulted.where: DEV.txt leaf 250-251, printed p. 215-216, s.v. Tambour
consulted.note: 'Le persan a la voyelle ou dans تبوراک taboûrâk, tambourin, lequel est, suivant toute vraisemblance, un diminutif de تبور tabour, dans lequel s'est glissé fautivement un ا â.' — confirms the word but makes it secondary, not the ancestor.
Horn's Grundriss has no article on the drum word.

nodes.derivation: Arabic طُنْبُور ṭunbūr is indeed an Iranian loan — Asbaghi lists tanbur among the Persian Musikinstrumente borrowed into Arabic, and Wiktionary derives the Arabic word 'from the Middle Persian ancestor of Classical Persian تنبور' — but not from this parent. ṭunbūr denotes a long-necked plucked LUTE, and its Persian ancestor is MP tambūr (Manichaean and Book Pahlavi), itself possibly a metathesis of Greek πανδοῦρα pandoûra 'three-stringed lute'. That is a different etymon from the drum word tabīr/tabūrāk of node #1: a percussion word and a chordophone word, with no shared derivation. Devic and Lammens saw this clearly — Lammens: 'il me semble difficile de dériver ce mot de l'arabe طنبور tonboûr, qui dans la langue classique ou parlée n'a jamais désigné qu'une lyre, guitare ou mandoline'. Nourai's own gloss ('a drum, ALSO a kind of stringed musical instrument') papers over the conflation.

nodes.derivation: Two words, both mis-routed. (a) تنبور tanbūr is not a re-borrowing from Arabic: it is the inherited Persian word, MP tambūr > NP tanbūr, and it is Arabic that took it, not the reverse. What IS a round trip is only the SPELLING طنبور with ط — Mo'in's own entry says so: 'تنبور [= دنبره = طنبور، معرّ.]', i.e. طنبور is the muʿarrab (Arabicised) orthography re-imported into Persian, exactly as with طبل below. (b) تنبک/دنبک tonbak has nothing to do with ṭunbūr at all: it continues MP tumbag/tumbak 'drum' (MacKenzie, Nyberg), an imitative word whose Armenian loan թմբուկ tʼmbuk < *tumbuk proves its Middle Iranian age; Nyberg expressly lists 'NP tanbak, tanbuk, tanbik' as its descendants. The chart's arrow would make an inherited Pahlavi word come back from Arabic in the Islamic period, which the Armenian evidence rules out.

nodes.derivation: The words are real but the parentage is wrong twice over. طُبُول ṭubūl is not an independent word: it is the broken plural of طَبْل ṭabl 'drum' (Klein: 'Arab. tabul, pl. of tabl'), and طَبّال ṭabbāl 'drummer' is the faʿʿāl occupational noun of the same root ط-ب-ل. And ṭabl does not come from ṭunbūr: Wiktionary derives it from 'Middle Iranian *tabir, tabil', Devic says flatly 'Tabl est d'origine persane', and Lokotsch (no. 1971) compares Hesychius' ταβάλα 'kettledrum' used by the Parthians. In other words ṭabl is the Arabic reflex of the very word in node #1 (tabīr/tabīl), so this box should hang from #1, not from the lute word #2; and the Arabicised singular, not a plural, is what the Persian box #5 continues.

nodes.derivation: NP طبل ṭabl 'drum' (with طبّال 'ṭabbāl, drummer') is an Arabic loan in Persian, and Nourai is right to draw it as a return arrow: the Arabic طبل itself goes back to a Middle Iranian *tabir/tabil, so طبل is a Persian→Arabic→Persian round trip (a muʿarrab re-import), which is exactly why it is written with ط and ب instead of a native Persian spelling, and why classical Persian keeps the older native تبیره beside it (Ferdowsī uses both). The agent noun طبّال is pure Arabic morphology (faʿʿāl) taken over whole.

nodes.derivation: A pass-through box with no word printed: the Old French link between the Arabic drum/lute words and English tambour. The form meant is OF tabour, tabur 'drum; din' (11th c., already in the Chanson de Roland: 'de tabours et de tymbres'), which by the 13th-14th c. was nasalised to tambour. The nasal is where Nourai's parent is defensible: Klein, AHD and Etymonline all say the m of tambour comes from the influence of Arabic ṭunbūr/ṭanbūr on an inherited tabour, so ṭunbūr is a real but partial parent — it shaped the word rather than supplied it. Wiktionary alone makes French tambour wholly 'from Arabic ṭunbūr', which is Nourai's reading.

nodes.derivation: The second empty Old French box is the un-nasalised branch: OF tabour, tabur 'drum; stool', the form behind English tabor and taboret. Etymonline backs Nourai's direct Persian parent — 'from Old French tabour, tabur “drum; din, noise, commotion” (11c.), probably from Persian tabir “drum”' — and Devic argued the same in 1876. The competing and commoner view routes it through Arabic: Klein and Lammens derive OF tabour from ṭabl/ṭubūl, Skeat and Wiktionary from ṭanbūr/ṭunbūr, both by way of Spanish atambor in the crusading and Andalusi contact zone. A Persian word reaching 11th-century France without an Arabic or Byzantine intermediary is historically improbable, so the arrow is acceptable only as shorthand.

nodes.derivation: E. tabor (also tabour) 'a small drum beaten with one hand while the other plays a pipe' is Middle English, borrowed from OF tabour; taboret / tabouret is French tabouret, the diminutive of the same OF tabour. The furniture sense Nourai glosses — 'a round low stool' — is the well-known metonymy: OF tabour already meant both 'drum' and 'stool' (Klein's gloss), because a drum-shaped, skin-topped seat looks like a small tabor; French tabouret has meant 'stool' since the 16th century, and English tabret is a variant of taboret. Both words are exactly where Klein and AHD put them.
